extracted.intended_audience: general public; students, researchers and policymakers interested in international development finance and the EBRD
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development's membership rules, governance, project approval process, financing instruments, environmental and human-rights policies, and limits on lending. Useful for understanding what makes projects/countries eligible and how decisions are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership eligibility (Articles of Agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: To become a member of the bank, a country needs to fit the EBRD's Articles of Agreement. These Articles stipulate that a country can only become a Member State if it is a state in Europe or a non-European member of the IMF. Institutions like the European Union and the EIB also participate in the bank operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership has expanded since foundation (including recent African accessions). The page lists capital subscriptions and dates for shareholders; membership implies representation on the Board of Governors and associated voting/ownership rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic lending eligibility (countries of operations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the EBRD has members worldwide, it only lends regionally in its countries of operations. Initially focused on former Eastern Bloc countries, it expanded to more than 30 countries from Central Europe to Central Asia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bank's regional remit determines borrower eligibility; historical expansion shows remit can evolve (e.g., moves into Asia and beyond).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/private sector lending split (public lending cap)
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of its lending policies, the EBRD mostly lends capital to the private sector; lending to the public sector is capped at 40% maximum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite public-sector shareholders, the bank invests primarily in private enterprises together with commercial partners. The public-sector cap shapes project selection and portfolio composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted financial instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: The bank provides different direct financial instruments such as loans, equity investments and guarantees, and assists SMEs through intermediaries (other banks or investment and venture capital funds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donor funding (grants, loans, risk-mitigating instruments) and partnerships (CIF, EU, GEF, GCF) complement EBRD instruments; choice of instrument depends on project type and objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project approval process (steps leading to a loan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each project is analysed: first by EBRD management with negotiations and the signing of a mandate letter drafting important information about the project plan, expected expenses, and responsibilities; then reviewed by management; later submitted to the Board of Directors for approval; after signing it becomes legally binding and leads to disbursement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stages: mandate-letter negotiation, internal management review, Board of Directors approval, contractual signing, fund transfer and repayment obligations. 'Conditions for disbursement' may apply and can prevent release of funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental mandate and coal exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBRD was the first multilateral development bank to have an explicit environmental mandate in its charter (since 1995) and will not finance thermal coal mining and coal-fired electricity generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bank adopted a Green Economy Transition (GET) approach and has tracked GET investment as a share of total investment. It pledged to dedicate above 40% of financing to green investment by 2020 (achieved in 2017) and aimed to become a majority green bank by 2025.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy sector strategy and decarbonisation
rubrics_metrics.description: EBRD's energy-sector strategy emphasizes decarbonisation and the switch from coal, placing decarbonisation at the centre of its energy policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical support includes corporate transition measures (examples: EV battery projects in Poland, elimination of plastics in Turkey, green retail in Ukraine). The bank's energy strategy shapes which energy projects are eligible for financing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political transformation, democracy and human-rights expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipient countries were expected to work towards 'multi-party democracy and political pluralism'; democracy and human-rights issues are integrated into the EBRD's founding agreement and operational approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EBRD has a Human Rights Working Group and internal human-rights guidance; it tracks and supports gender inclusion (noting increases in projects promoting gender inclusion). Political and human-rights considerations can influence engagement with particular countries and projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for disbursement and environmental/social safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects may be subject to specific conditions for disbursement (e.g., environmental safeguards); if conditions are not met, the bank can cancel or suspend funding — 'conditions for disbursement were not met' has been cited as reason to cancel loans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Boskov Most dam loan was cancelled after the Standing Committee of the Bern Convention raised biodiversity concerns; UNESCO/ICOMOS/IUCN monitoring and NGO objections have led to suspension or cancellation of projects. Environmental and social impact monitoring and mitigation measures are expected and can be grounds for withholding funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance structure and decision powers (Board roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBRD has a three-tier governance structure: the president and staff; the Board of Governors (representatives from each member state with authority power); and the Board of Directors (23 members elected by the Board of Governors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board of Directors functions include approving the budget; establishing policies and making decisions on loans and investments (in accordance with the Board of Governors); preparing the work of the Board of Governors; and submitting audited accounts yearly. Voting rights differ by member geography and capital subscription, with European and creditor members holding majority voting power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions, suspension and country-specific policy responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBRD can suspend access to its resources for entities from particular countries and close offices in response to geopolitical events (e.g., suspension of new investment projects in Russia in 2014; suspension of resource access for Russian and Belarusian entities and office closures in 2022).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such measures are taken by Governing bodies (Board of Governors/Board decisions) in response to international policy developments and can apply to new projects while ongoing projects may be managed differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donor funding sources and uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Donors provide funds to support EBRD activities in the form of grants, loans and risk-mitigating instruments, with donors including bilateral partners, the Climate Investment Funds, the European Union, the Global Environment Facility and the Green Climate Fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donor funds support initiatives such as the Resilience Framework, Trade Facilitation Programme and Vital Infrastructure Support Programme, and are reported in EBRD sustainability and annual reports.
